The classical kemençe is a pear-shaped, three-string bowed instrument descended from the medieval Greek Byzantine lyra, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-71, a chordophone of the violin family. The body, pegbox and neck are made from a single piece of wood, the soundboard has two D-shaped soundholes, there is no nut, and the strings are stopped with the side of the fingernail. It is played seated, held between the knees or on one knee with the head up, using a bow called the yay or doksar. It is used mainly by the Greeks of Asia Minor and in classical Ottoman music, and also in the early Smyrna-style rebetiko; from the middle of the nineteenth century it became the main bowed instrument of Ottoman classical music, and it is still played.
古典肯曼切琴源自中世紀希臘拜占庭里拉琴；其名「肯曼切」來自波斯語卡曼恰，意為小弓: The classical kemençe comes from the medieval Greek Byzantine lyra; its name comes from the Persian kamancheh, meaning little bow, while lyra goes back to the ancient Greek lyre. The Byzantine lyra was described by the Persian geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih (died 911) as a typical Byzantine instrument. The instrument was used early in popular music, such as the early Smyrna-style rebetiko, and by Greek immigrants from Asia Minor, and it entered classical Ottoman music. After the middle of the nineteenth century it became the main bowed instrument of Ottoman classical music and is still played; variants of the same shape and playing method exist around the Mediterranean and the Balkans.

It sounds when the bow rubs the strings; the strings are stopped not with the fingertip but with the side of the nail, as on some folk bowed instruments from southeastern Europe to South Asia. Beginners can first practise holding the body steady and controlling the direction of the bow, then stop the strings with the side of the nail to fix the pitch.
